newsitem.title: USA: Yale cites Salmonella in fighting cancer.
newsitem.headline: Yale cites Salmonella in fighting cancer.

text.p: Researchers at the Yale School of Medicine have identified Salmonella as a possible means of fighting cancer.
"It's potentially a huge step forward," Yale cancer biologist Dr. John Pawelek told Reuters on Tuesday.
Pawelek said his team had genetically altered the food-poisoning bacterium to seek out and destroy tumors in mice.
Yale has licensed the project to New Haven-based Vion Pharmaceuticals Inc to develop a clinical product.
Vion said in a press release on Monday that it anticipated clinical trials in humans by the middle of next year.
Pawelek said the Salmonella treatment was promising because it worked like a seek-and-destroy missile against tumors.
"In our opinion, it's revolutionary," Pawelek said. "What we really have done is developed a vector (delivery mechanism) which is the Salmonella, which we have modified so that it's safe."
"It's a vector that travels from distant sites to tumors. If you introduce it into the blood stream of a mouse that bears tumors at multiple sites in its body, the Salmonella will seek them out."
"There is no other vector like that, as far as we know."
The researchers also found that the same Salmonella strains could also prevent the growth of tumors, Pawelek said.
"Our goal was not just to develop those vectors, but then to be able to insert other, toxic genes into them that could affect the growth of the tumor as well."
"So we have developed a two-pronged vector here, that on its own is very good at holding back tumors, and also is a delivery vehicle for bringing whatever we want to the tumors."
Pawelek, an expert in melanoma biology, said the Salmonella strains could potentially be used to fight cancers of the skin, breast, colon, prostate, liver and lung.
"It really seems to work for virtually all solid tumors," he said.
